assessment.nobel_worthiness: Random-coefficients demand estimation with endogenous prices and product characteristics (Berry; Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes), together with Pakes's dynamic oligopoly and estimation work, became the standard toolkit for merger review, antitrust and empirical trade and IO. The contribution is both a method and a framework, which is the combination I value.
assessment.attribution: The BLP core is a compact, well-identified three-person contribution. Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin are important but more peripheral to the central demand-estimation breakthrough, so I exclude them from the proposed laureates.
assessment.maturity: The core papers date from 1994-1995, and three decades of use in policy and across fields give high confirmation and a long track record.
uncertainties: The three-name limit forces the exclusion of Bresnahan and others whose work on market power and identification is foundational.
Whether the Committee treats this as an IO or an econometrics contribution could affect its standing.
I cannot independently verify citation or adoption figures here.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Kiyotaki-Moore's model of collateral constraints that amplify and propagate shocks is a foundational mechanism for credit cycles. It underlies much modern macro-finance, including work on crises and financial frictions in DSGE models.
assessment.attribution: The central 1997 paper has two authors and clear credit. Gertler and Gilchrist are important for the financial accelerator and its empirics, but the accelerator was already central to the 2022 prize through Bernanke. I credit the two originators of the collateral-constraint mechanism.
assessment.maturity: The mechanism has been tested and extended for over 25 years, and the 2008 crisis reinforced its relevance. Timing is mature.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize (Bernanke) may weigh against, or in favour of, a second financial-frictions award.
Whether Gertler should be included alongside Kiyotaki and Moore is a judgment call.
Direct empirical identification of the collateral mechanism is less clean than the theory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The heterogeneous-firm trade model changed how trade is analysed. It explains exporter selection, reallocation within industries, and a new channel for welfare gains. It reoriented empirical work built on firm-level data and extends the new trade theory recognised in 2008.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the pivotal paper, and Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple (2004) and Helpman's broader theory work add to it. Redding's contributions to quantitative and spatial trade are significant but a distinct strand, so I do not include him.
assessment.maturity: Two decades of testing against firm-level data and extensions give high confirmation. Some quantitative results are sensitive to functional-form assumptions.
uncertainties: Credit allocation among Helpman, Melitz and others who contributed to heterogeneous-firm trade (for example Bernard, Eaton, Jensen, Kortum) is not settled by this list.
Possible Committee preference for a different trade strand, such as quantitative Ricardian models or political economy of trade.
Welfare conclusions depend on structural assumptions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework with nominal rigidities and interest-rate rules is the intellectual basis of modern monetary policy analysis and central-bank practice. Its policy influence is exceptional.
assessment.attribution: This is the hardest attribution on the list. Many contributors (Calvo, Taylor, Christiano-Eichenbaum-Evans, Smets-Wouters, Gertler, Gali, Woodford) are credited, and any three is arbitrary. I propose Woodford and Gali for the integrated theory and Taylor for rules and staggered contracts, accepting that important names are left out.
assessment.maturity: The framework is mature and tested over decades through crises and policy regimes. It has also been challenged, notably by HANK models and by the post-2021 inflation episode.
uncertainties: Three-name cap versus an eight-name list makes attribution contestable.
Taylor and Calvo's priority claims may compete with the synthesis authors.
Some evidence has weakened parts of the framework, such as the New Keynesian Phillips curve fit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The alternating-offers bargaining model (Rubinstein 1982) is a cornerstone of game theory and of applications in labour, trade, political economy and search. Its key result, a unique subgame-perfect equilibrium, is elegant and has been widely used.
assessment.attribution: Rubinstein's 1982 paper is the central contribution and attribution is relatively clear. Binmore and Wolinsky built on or extended it (the Binmore-Rubinstein-Wolinsky link to markets and the Nash program), so I propose Rubinstein alone as the primary credit.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with more than four decades of use as a canonical model.
uncertainties: Whether the Committee would include Wolinsky or Binmore for the market-bargaining extension.
Empirical content is more limited than for the other leading candidates.
Pure game theory has recent Nobel coverage (auction and mechanism design), which may affect timing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The China-shock work shows large, persistent local labour-market effects of import competition, and the task-based analysis of technology reshaped how we think about wage inequality and polarisation. It has strong empirical credibility and policy relevance, and it links labour, trade and technology.
assessment.attribution: The China shock studies are by Autor, Dorn and Hanson. The earlier task-approach and technology work involves Autor with Katz, Levy and Murnane, and Acemoglu's related work was recognised in 2024. Credit across the two strands is partly overlapping.
assessment.maturity: The core papers date from 2013 onwards, with subsequent replications and refinements, so long-run effects are fairly well measured. Some debate continues about magnitudes and identification.
uncertainties: Shift-share identification has been debated.
Overlap with the 2024 recognition of Acemoglu on technology and institutions.
Possible Committee view that the work is more recent than comparable laureate-level contributions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative data have transformed measurement of intergenerational mobility, neighbourhood effects and causal place effects, with major policy influence. It fits my view that new data together with a conceptual framework make a contribution.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is central across the programme, and Hendren co-leads the neighbourhood causal-effects work (Chetty-Hendren). Katz's earlier Moving to Opportunity work and Friedman's collaboration are important but I keep the credit narrower. Because the line of work is team-based, attribution is the main difficulty.
assessment.maturity: The work is relatively recent (about 2014 onwards) and some results are still being replicated and debated, so confirmation is still partial.
uncertainties: Possible premature timing relative to other candidates.
Debate over methodology of the neighbourhood-effects estimates and over mobility measurement.
Large collaborative teams make selecting two names difficult.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Machine-learning methods for causal inference (double/debiased machine learning, causal forests, heterogeneous effects) extend the credibility revolution to high-dimensional settings and are now widely applied across applied fields. The methodological contribution is substantial.
assessment.attribution: Chernozhukov's double machine learning, and Athey and Wager's causal forests and related work, are distinct but complementary strands. Chernozhukov is also credited on quantile methods elsewhere on the list. Credit among the three is reasonably identifiable.
assessment.maturity: The key papers are from roughly 2016-2018, so the track record is short compared with the other ranked candidates. Adoption is fast, but long-run influence is not yet established, and causal-inference methods were recognised in 2021.
uncertainties: Time since the core work may be too short for a prize.
Overlap with the 2021 prize for causal inference (Angrist, Imbens).
Other contributors to the double machine learning and causal ML literature are not on this list.
